summary: Argues that mail senders should be able to assign a priority to messages, as suggested in RFC 539. It answers an objection in RFC 555 that urgency levels need defined effects on the mail server, noting that people, not programs, will usually pick the priority and may do so inconsistently.

plainLanguage.summary: Should you be able to mark a letter urgent? He says yes, even though people may not agree on what urgent means.

questions: mail priority in early arpanet mail
subtitle: Argues for allowing users to assign priority levels to mail messages.

tldr.problem: Some messages are more urgent than others, but early mail protocols did not allow senders to indicate importance to recipients.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal is to add a priority field to mail messages, allowing senders to mark messages with a numeric urgency level from 0 (junk mail) to 10 (phone in the middle of the night). Though humans may not consistently assign priorities, including the information gives recipients a way to manage urgent messages.
tldr.outcome: Priority levels provide a way for senders to communicate urgency, and allow mail servers and human recipients to decide how to handle messages based on that information. While perfect consistency may be impossible, the feature is fundamentally useful.

facts.label: Highest urgency (10)
facts.value: Phone in the middle of the night, if necessary

today: RFC 577 presents an argument and design suggestion for mail priority. It is not a specification or standard, but an early contribution to email protocol design.

sections.title: The Case for Priority
sections.content: An earlier proposal (RFC 539) suggested that mail senders be able to assign a priority to their messages. Jim White objected in RFC 555, arguing that urgency levels are meaningless without defined effects on the mail server. This RFC responds by noting that while human senders may not be perfectly consistent in assigning priorities, the concept of urgency is fundamental to communication. Excluding it from the protocol would be a loss.
sections.plainLanguage: One person said mail should have urgency levels. Another said that doesn't make sense unless the mail system does something specific with them. The author agrees urgency is real and people will use it, even if imperfectly.

sections.title: Priority Levels and Their Meanings
sections.content: The RFC suggests a scale from 0 to 10, with suggested interpretations for automated messages. Level 10 means phone the recipient in the middle of the night if necessary. Level 8 means deliver to the user's terminal immediately. Level 6 means deliver only if the user is at the command level. Level 4 means deliver after sign-on or before sign-off. Level 2 means deliver to the standard mailbox. Level 0 means junk mail. Intermediate levels are available for fine-grained distinction. The proposal notes that automated programs (like notification systems) can use these suggested values to communicate message importance, even though human senders may be inconsistent.
sections.plainLanguage: From 10 (wake them up!) to 0 (garbage), the numbers tell the receiver how much to care about a message.

sections.title: Why Urgency Matters
sections.content: The author emphasizes that urgency is a fundamental part of human communication. While automated systems cannot guarantee consistent priority assignment, the simple inclusion of priority information in the mail protocol is valuable. Individual humans and servers can interpret the urgency levels however they see fit. The benefit of having the information available outweighs the cost of inconsistent human judgment.
sections.plainLanguage: Even if people don't always mark things correctly, having a way to say something is important is better than having no way to say it at all.
